In this lesson, you will learn about thermo-electronic devices, heat transducers.
INTRODUCTIONM
These devices, when combined with common electronic circuits, produce heat circuits that have many uses.
For example, large computer systems use heat sensors to determine the operating temperature.
If the equipment becomes too hot, the sensors turn on fans or
air-conditioning units to lower the temperature..
Other electronic systems may use heat generators and heat sensors to heat up the equipment.
High power radio transmitters normally operate at temperatures above room temperature. They need heaters to warm them before use.

As stated, all electronic components with resistance will heat up as current flows through the circuit.
A measure of how much heat is generated is a component's thermal resistance, qR.
qR equates electrical watts to the temperature within the core of the device and is rated as degrees C per electrical watt.
qR is given by the manufacturer and is used to determine how hot the core of a component will get depending on the amount of power applied.

When components heat up the heat must be dissipated before damage occurs.
This process, called dissipation, is accomplished using a heat sink, a material in contact with the heat source.
Heat sinks lower the core temperature of the heat source and facilitate heat transfer to the surrounding air.
When a heating device uses a heat sink, qR is replaced with qja. qja is the total thermal resistance from the core of the component to air.
qja is lower than qR, this reduces the heating devices core temperature. This reduction raises the amount of power that can be applied.
The value of qja depends on the type of component, case and heat sink used.
The total thermal resistance is equal to the sum of the individual thermal resistances.
Where qjc is the thermal resistance of the component's core to case.
qsc is the thermal resistance of the case to heat sink.
qsa is the thermal resistance of the heat sink to air.

Heat sensors are either resistive, current, or voltage devices.
DISCUSSION
These types of sensors are electrical in nature and produce outputs that are calibrated to indicate temperature in Fahrenheit (F), Celsius (C), or Kelvin (K).
Before looking at electrical sensors, let's see how the more familiar mechanical heat sensors operate..
The thermometer is a common device used to sense heat......
Liquid mercury fills a reservoir and expands or contracts at a rate of about .01% per degree F.
As temperature increases, the mercury is pushed up the hollow stem due to expansion. When temperature decreases, the mercury falls down the stem due to contraction..
The scale on the hollow stem is marked in F, C, or K.
A Filled System Thermometer, a Bourdon Tube, uses a liquid or gas in a spiral tube.
As the liquid gas heats up or cools off, the spiral expands or contracts causing the pointer to move.
The Bi-metallic thermometers bend two dissimilar metals into a spiral. They are normally used in home thermometers..
The two metals expand and contract at different rates according to the temperature, thus moving the pointer.
Again, the scale is marked in F, C, or K.
The Filled System and the Bi-metallic thermometers can have the pointer connected to a potentiometer for use in electrical circuits.
What principle do mechanical heat sensors operate on?
Voltage and current are electrical properties. Mechanical sensors do not operate using electrical properties.
TRY AGAIN!
Hot and cold are human terms used to describe temperature. All heat sensors sense hot and cold but in terms of temperature.
TRY AGAIN!
Now, let's look at four electrical heat sensors............
The thermo-couple, TC, is a voltage heat sensor.
It is the simplest of the electrical sensors and was discovered in 1812.
The thermo-couple is nothing more than two dissimilar metal wires intertwined at one end.
When heat is applied to the twisted end, electrons in one of the metals tend to move away from the heat, to the free end.
This produces a negative charge on the free end of the metal pieces.
At the same time, electrons in the other metal tend to move toward the heat, to the twisted end.
This produces a positive charge on the free end of the other metal piece.
The result is a small difference in potential across the two open ends depending on the amount of heat, this is a variable voltage source.
Thermo-couplers are rated in mV/F and depending on the types of metals used have various ranges.
Fahrenheit the output signal is only 50 mV.
Since TC's have very small output voltages op-amps are normally used to boost the signal.
A thermistor (TH) is a heat sensitive resistor. This is a resistive heat sensor..
Thermistors are made of oxides consisting of nickel, manganese, cobalt, and copper.
TH's have negative temperature coefficients. This means as temperature increases, resistance decreases and when temperature decreases, resistance increases.
Comparing a thermistor to a thermo-couple, you can see that output, R, is not linear and the range of temperature are less than the TC. TC.
Because of the non-linear output, most thermistors use a scale similar to VOM ohmmeter scales.
Thermistors are used in circuits that sense temperatures between -150
F. They are very sensitive to temperature changes..
Circuits that use thermistors use the resistance of the device to control current flow.
By scaling an ammeter, you can get direct readouts of temperature in F, C, or K.
The resistance temperature detector (RTD) is very similar to the thermistor (TH). It also is a resistive heat sensor.
RTDs are made of pure metals such as platinum, copper, and nickel.
The difference is that RTDs have a positive temperature coefficient. This means as temperature increases, resistance increases and when temperature decreases, resistance decreases..
RTDs have a more linear output and are more sensitive to temperature changes than THs.
The temperature range is only from approximately -100 degrees F to 400 degrees F.
Circuits that use RTDs are similar to TH circuits, only a more complex design is needed due to the 0.3% sensitivity.
The final heat sensor is the solid state sensor, TD. They are current heat sensor devices..
The solid state heat sensor is nothing more than a diode...
TDs operate by using the reverse bias leakage current.
All reverse biased PN junctions exhibit leakage current. The leakage current is proportional to temperature.
By using this property, a diode is easily used as a heat sensor.
Silicon diodes double the leakage current for each 6 degrees C of temperature change.
While Germanium diodes double leakage current for every 10 degrees C of temperature change.
Circuits that use diodes as temperature sensors normally use an amplifier due to the small values of leakage current.
An ammeter can be used to indicate temperature. Remember, heat sensors are current diodes.
